Tell us how you heard about Zipline and this job!

Tell us about your experience collaborating with cross-functional teams (e.g., civil, mechanical, electrical, software, operations, etc.). What was your role, and how did you contribute to the team's success?
entries.value: At SnapSort, an AI photo-sorting product I founded, I built the application from zero using Flask, AWS, and a multi-model inference pipeline, and I also recruited and led a small cross-functional team across product, marketing, and operations. My role was technical owner plus the person who had to translate between functions: the marketing side needed to know which sorting behaviors were actually reliable enough to promise, and operations needed to know what happened when inference failed on a large upload. I grew it to more than 300 users and raised roughly $5,000 in non-dilutive funding, and I owned pricing and positioning alongside the code. The biggest thing I learned was that a technically functional system and a product people actually use are very different things, and most of that gap got closed in conversations with non-engineers. I had similar experience on the Gates Foundation health-equity project, where I was lead model developer and worked directly with the principal investigator on variable selection and model specification, which meant constantly translating between what XGBoost and SHAP were telling me and the substantive public-health question the team cared about.

entries.label: Tell us about a time you created documentation that helped engineers or technicians perform a task, follow a process, or troubleshoot an issue. What was the outcome?
entries.value: On the jobright-application-agent, a Playwright-based job-application agent I built in TypeScript and Node, the documentation was the product in a real sense. Browser automation is dangerous here because one wrong action can submit a real application or fill a legal field incorrectly, so I wrote down an explicit state machine (DISCOVERED, ELIGIBILITY_CHECK, QUEUED, INSPECT, FILL, READY_TO_SUBMIT, SUBMITTING, SUBMITTED, OUTREACH, COMPLETED) and documented which environment flags gate each mutating capability, including SUBMIT_ENABLED and FORM_FILL_ENABLED, along with the rule that they never default to enabled. I also documented a validation ladder: UNIT_CONFIRMED, FIXTURE_CONFIRMED, LIVE_READ_ONLY_CONFIRMED, LIVE_MUTATION_CONFIRMED. The point was that no one, including me, gets to call a capability working just because it passed against a local fixture. The outcome was that when something broke during a live run, I could locate the failure by state rather than guessing, and I made deliberate decisions to detect and skip Workday, iCIMS, and Oracle instead of handling them unreliably. I also built an operator console, Dispatch, so the documented pipeline was observable rather than just described on paper.
